utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness there. Let him make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Kotur, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you introduce yourself to us, please, and tell us your movements in your service, what education you've had, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: My name is Milan Kotur. I was born on the 23rd of September, 1947 in Indjija. That is Vojvodina province, in the Republic of Serbia. [French on English channel] school, secondary school of the science stream. I went to the military academy for the ground forces, the infantry. I completed the academy after four years, and the first rank I was given was as a 2nd lieutenant and sent to the 2nd Army district in Zagreb to take up my duties. In addition to the military academy, I went to the staff academy for two years and have completed the highest schools, military schools - the School of National Defence in particular -- and in addition to that several courses, the most important of which was the sabotage course, the intelligence course, and superior intelligence course. And the duties that I performed included the commander of reconnaissance units, a regiment officer, and of my command duties, battalion commander and brigade commander were the most important posts. And of the operative duties, I was Chief of Staff of the brigade, chief of the department for operative affairs in the corps, and chief of the department of the armed forces when I was -- when I retired last March. I have been in -- working in ten garrisons. I worked in ten garrisons during my service: Zagreb, Varazdin, Koprivnica, Leskovac, Kursumlija being among them, as well as Kosovska Mitrovica, Pristina once again until I was sent to Leskovac and Novi Sad, and I retired in Novi Sad from my duties there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, you said you were born in Indjija. Could you tell us, please, whether your family lived in Indjija for a long time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: My parents, after World War II, came to Indjija in 1946. Otherwise, they had lived in Croatia, on the territory of Croatia, that is to say in the Kordun area and the Lika region. And during the Second World War my family suffered a great deal, both on my mother's side and my father's side in the Independent State of Croatia, at the time as it was called. Several hundred thousand people lost their lives for the simple fact of not being Croats. And later on my parents moved to Indjija, and my other relatives remained living in Croatia where, in 1995, under the effects of the armed forces of Croatia and the so-called Operation Storm, they withdrew to Serbia, moved to Serbia, and today live -- went from Sid, Nova Batajnica, Novi Pazar, Zemun and so on and settled in that general area. Right down to Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, what your job was in Kosovo and Metohija, and I'm thinking of the period just prior to the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: As far as my basic duties were concerned, before the war and during the war I was chief of infantry in the command of the Pristina Corps. However, before the war, pursuant to an order of the Pristina Corps dated the 23rd of October, I was sent to be a member of the team of the Pristina Corps that numbered five officers and which had the task of realising the tasks of the Pristina Corps emanating from the contents of an agreement between OSCE and NATO in Kosovo for Kosovo and Metohija, and I was at the head of that particular team. At the beginning of the war, I headed another team that had as its assignment to control and monitor the units which had taken up positions in the defence area and closed off the axis from Macedonia towards Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's dwell for a moment on your assignment. You said you were the head of a team which was appointed by the Pristina Corps to maintain ties and liaisons with the OSCE Verification Mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have here a large number of documents. Are all these documents in fact the product of your activities as part of the team and as head of the team, in fact, which was appointed to maintain relations with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: All the documents that are there are the product of the work of my team during the period while the Verification Mission was in Kosovo and Metohija. I was the liaison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms could you explain us to the Kosovo Verification Mission; how it functioned, its set-up and organisation. And in tab 2 you will find a schematic, a diagram of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The Kosovo Verification Mission, at the head of the mission was Mr. Walker, and he was head of mission. He had its executive secretariat and his council and his assistants. He had assistants for the police, for political questions, a political advisor, he had a staff advisor. He had Mr. Keller for politics, Drewienkiewicz for operational matters, and he had Mr. Bochard [phoen], Bochard, whom -- I'm not sure what particular job he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, were you fully acquainted with the contents of the agreement governing the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with the agreement of the Verification Mission in Kosovo and Metohija, and particularly as it related to the solving of the crisis in Kosovo. In October 1998, the 26th of October, in fact, agreement was signed in Belgrade on the Verification Mission for Kosovo by the federal ministry of Yugoslavia and the presiding organ for security and cooperation, which envisaged that the OSCE should establish a Verification Mission, and had established a Verification Mission in Kosovo and Metohija, including Yugoslavia's obligations to abide by the Resolution 1160 and 1199, those two Resolutions. There was also an agreement of the 15th of October in Belgrade which was signed by the Chief of Staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the main commanding officer for Europe of the NATO alliance, which envisaged the establishment of a Verification Mission of Kosovo in the air as an addition to the OSCE Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpreters and the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and the Colonel, you're being asked to speak more slowly by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kotur, in view of the fact that you were at the head of the team of the Pristina Corps, could you tell us, please, briefly, what the duties were of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Pursuant to a decision made by the federal organs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, an order was issued throughout Kosovo and Metohija that the number of security forces should be reduced. That is to say the MUP forces and the forces of the army of Yugoslavia, and their equipment and materiel to the general normal level, that is to say the level before terrorist activity broke out, with the intention of creating conditions conducive to the speedy revival of the political process to settle all unsettled humanitarian and political issues. All the units of the army of Yugoslavia and all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're speaking at the same speed, and I can hear it in the interpreter's voice they're struggling to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the units of the army of Yugoslavia and all the additional equipment and materiel brought into Kosovo and Metohija after February 1998 was withdrawn from Kosovo and Metohija. The Pristina Corps, since it covered the overall territory, geographically speaking, of Kosovo and Metohija, and all the duties and obligations that stemmed from the agreement of the OSCE mission and NATO were implemented by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us briefly, please, whether the Pristina Corps fulfilled all its obligations emanating from the agreement reached with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps fully complied with all the undertakings on the basis of the agreement signed with the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was responsible for the security of the members of the mission and how -- what was your conduct like vis-a-vis their members, the members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The Verification Mission was established in conformity and agreement with the federal government of Yugoslavia, and it was also established in Kosovo and Metohija under full government guarantees which were provided for their security and safety, along with our responsibility to guarantee the safety and security of their members fully. There were diplomatic missions which -- enjoying diplomatic immunity, and our conduct towards them was fully in keeping with the Geneva Convention governing diplomatic agreements between countries from which their privileges emanated and their immunity emanated and the obligations we took on to provide full and complete safety and security for their members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, during the time the Verification Mission spent in Kosovo and Metohija, was this obligation fully realised? That is to say was their security and safety realised fully? Were there any incidents that broke out which jeopardised or threatened the mission and its members? I'm talking about the conduct of the police, the army, the citizens in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: There were no incidents which would jeopardise the mission, and the security forces abided by their obligation to guarantee their security and safety until they withdrew in 1999 on the 20th of March. We communicated with them, we had direct contacts on an everyday basis at the headquarters in Pristina and in the regional centres and the coordination centres. We had contacts through communication channels, we had special links with them, and mobile telephones, PTT communications, et cetera. Then during their activities in the border area we had communications with them, and also we looked into the causes and consequences of incidents, and we had cooperation with the mission with the anti-defence systems of the Pristina Corps, and that is in accordance with NATO regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You brought a map here, which is in tab 6 and which shows where parts of the mission were in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good idea to have a look at it. Can I put it here? What we see here now is the area of Kosovo and Metohija, and all the organs of the Kosovo Verification Mission are depicted here as organised in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The headquarters of the mission were in Pristina. They had coordination centres in the main towns of various regions like Kosovo Mitrovica, Pec, Prizren, Gnjilane and Pristina. Every Regional Centre covered a zone which was roughly like the zone of the districts in Kosovo and Metohija. Then Glina, Djakovica, Decani. Not to go into all of that, these are the black dots here. And in every bigger town they had their offices or, rather, their forward posts. You can see here that the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija was covered with organs of the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next map or, rather, in tab 7, you have a diagram of communication among the various teams. Chart of communications between the teams and liaison officers of the 3rd Army in the OSCE mission. Can you explain that, how it functioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This is a chart of communication between the teams and liaison officers of the 3rd Army and the OSCE mission. We see the chain of command. It went down the chain of command. In the general staff, we had a team that liaised with the mission, and then the 3rd commander was in Nis and they liaised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, the interpreters have once again asked me to request that you speak more slowly. Apparently you're a fast speaker, so you have to exercise some --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The command of the Pristina Corps had a liaison office and I headed it. And then liaison officers in garrisons were linked to that team. In Pristina, Kosovska Mitrovica, Djakovica, Prizren, Urosevac, Gnjilane, and Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these garrisons that were roughly at brigade level and regiment level?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes. Regiment and brigade level. As for the team of the Pristina Corps, it also included officers in commands of the border battalions; 23rd -- 53rd, 55th, and 57th, with its seats in Djakovica, the 53rd, the 55th was in Prizren, and the 57th in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: And the team of the Pristina Corps had constant communication with the Verification Mission in Pristina. And the command of the 3rd Army did the same thing, but from time to time. That is depicted by the arrows here on the chart. And the Verification Mission in Pristina also had different regional coordination centres that were in the seats of the different districts. Pristina, Pec, Kosovska Mitrovica, Prizren, and Gnjilane. I've already indicated that on the map. These regional coordination centres can be seen on this map. That is a good thing. In order to understand better how well spread out the mission was, they had different groups for weapons and for other activities. They also had inspection teams for inspecting military bases and arms; 23 at that. Then teams for monitoring interior borders, from 12 to 15. Investigation teams for investigating incidents and cease-fire violations. A verification group for border operations, and teams for monitoring the border with Albania and Macedonia. As for the chain of command, the team of the Pristina Corps was linked to the team of the 3rd Army, and the team of the 3rd Army to the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia and Belgrade. The team of the General Staff for liaison with missions in Belgrade liaised with the OSCE liaison office in Belgrade. That is again shown with these arrows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope that you have now fully explained the structure and organisation of the Verification Mission and your relations with them. Tell me, what was the cooperation with the mission like?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The cooperation with the mission, well, first and foremost, my relations with the mission were based on mutual respect and confidence. I considered them to be full partners in order to achieve a full democratic solution on the basis of the full equality of all citizens in Kosovo and Metohija. We had some misunderstandings in interpreting some agreements and in other matters, but I think that on our part all the contacts were very correct and they never went outside this particular framework.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The framework of --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Correctness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And good relations.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, how did the verifiers behave when meeting up with the military?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The verifiers behaved correctly to a large extent, and there was also some behaviour when there was a bit of provocation involved, a bit of lack of understanding, especially when they wanted to enter the border areas unannounced, enter barracks and see units that were in this area. Then there were some provocative questions, like, "What are you doing there? There is no place for you here. Can your commander not talk to us?" Then they tried to enter some unit premises by force, by removing barriers. Cases like that. That's what happened during the stay of the mission in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said just now, does that mean that they were always announced when they would come, or was that not always the case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That was not always the case, and that is why often such things happened. Well, small incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the established organisation, did you have some kind of agreement on this, how you should communicate, how they should be announced in order for them to carry out their obligations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: As early as the first meeting we had with them, we explained the structure of our organs existing in Kosovo and Metohija with a view to carrying out this agreement, and also in terms of their relationship, both with their centres on the ground and also our own liaison officers. Also, our team and the Pristina Corps liaised with the mission in Pristina itself. We agreed that all contacts that should take place in this area would have to be announced 24 hours in advance. In the beginning, this was not really observed, because they had a very rigid method, a very aggressive, arrogant method in terms of their approach. Quite simply, they ignored this agreement. The moment when they stopped behaving that way, our cooperation became far more efficient and better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had daily meetings with the verifiers. What were the items on the agenda of these meetings and what kind of problems did you encounter and did you manage to resolve them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Everything that happened in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija was on the agenda of our daily meetings. All incidents, all situations that cropped up that required explanations, all requests that the verifiers had with a view to controlling units and visiting them were discussed at these meetings. And we managed to resolve practically all of these questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attended these daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: These daily meetings that we had with the representatives of the OSCE mission were always attended by someone from the team who took the minutes, or in Pristina we also had an office of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, the federal ministry, numbering nine to 11 people. So sometimes there would be a person from the Foreign Ministry who would be taking the minutes, and also there would be an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation like in relation to the verifiers entering the border area? What was the position of the verifiers? What did they ask from you and what was the agreement like in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: In accordance with the agreement between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the OSCE, the border units remained in the border area in order to secure the state border, as well as all units that were providing in-depth security of the state border, and they stayed in place. The border area was expanded by about five kilometres, and all these forces, the border forces and the in-depth security units were in this border belt. In this border belt there is a special regimen which was regulated by the rules of border service. Since all units in the border area are armed and have ammunition, this is probably the only peacetime task that is carried out in combat conditions. That is why it is very important to protect the safety and security of people, of the population there or the verifiers - we're discussing the verifiers now. It was very important not to go in unannounced or without a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was the only request from your side that a liaison officer be present when they enter the border area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That was our only request, for the sake of the safety of the verifiers so that their mission or their request that had to do with the population or inspecting the border units, all the things that they were entitled to. We just wanted them to be announced, and this could only be carried out through a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, where is this evidence taking us? How does it relate to the charges in the indictment? I can see the relevance of -- of it to a certain degree, but it's not clear to me why we need to spend so much time on the Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because the Verification Mission played a certain role in preparing the war against Yugoslavia, and I want this to be shown through the testimony of the man who headed the Pristina Corps team and who cooperated with them. Secondly, several members of the Verification Mission testified here, and I'm going to ask him about the claims they made during the course of giving evidence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I'd like to hear, because I think we have had enough background information on the work of the Verification Mission. So if you would proceed to that part of the evidence, I think that would be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll move through this very quickly and get to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Kotur, here's a question for you, a general question: Was the Verification Mission objective? Do you think that they reported as things really happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I could not be sure that the mission was objective in its reporting. When taking into account the complete work of the mission, the overall work of the mission, and where they spent a lot of their time, I came to the conclusion that they were not always fair and correct and that they did not only have that intention, to verify what happened, but they also tried to get us into some kind of parallel relations or, rather, relations between the KLA and the military. They wanted to turn us into partners in all of this. And this attitude towards the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, they were very benevolent towards them. So when I take all of this into account, especially some events like Racak and some others, I could not claim that -- that their reporting was quite truthful, fully truthful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's put it this way: Roughly we have three protagonists here: You have the Verification Mission, you have the KLA, and our organs. What was your conclusion on the relations that were established there within that triangle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, why is the Verification Mission described as a protagonist? Will his evidence substantiate that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite simply, it is one of the protagonists, one of the entities that was active in Kosovo and Metohija at the time, and it has relations with our authorities, as was originally envisaged, but then they established some relations with the KLA as well. I'm asking Colonel Kotur to give us his observations in relation to these relations. It really exists. I imagine that there is no need to prove that, that the mission exists, that it works, that there is an agreement on the basis of which it is supposed to operate, and now let us see how it operates in relation to the agreement and what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let the colonel answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The attitude of the mission towards the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army was a rather benevolent one, if I am to put it in a single sentence. They had their representative, their permanent representative in the headquarters of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, and often their statements and their requests were fully being taken into account without any kind of verification or double checking, whereas our side always had to prove that they had not done something or that they had done something if that was the case. Their interpretation was that the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army was not sufficiently organised and was not under a single command, and that it lacks discipline and that, therefore, the requirements of them could not be like those from us. That would be it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As far as general questions go, I'll ask you one concerning the attitude and the conduct of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Could you tell us briefly what misunderstandings existed with the KVM regarding the interpretation of the agreement concerning their mandate and especially the methods of their work, as briefly you can.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: They believed, as far as methods of work are concerned, that they have an unlimited choice of methods available to them, as well as unlimited freedom of movement. Nobody contested their freedom of movement. There were only restrictions regarding the border belt. As for the method they chose, and that was the right to inspect any unit they chose, units armed with 12.7-millimetre calibre weapons upwards, they thought they were entitled to enter into installation, inspect any unit, and use their technology to determine the exact location of every feature, every installation. According to our interpretation of our agreement with the OSCE, we did not think that they were entitled to do that, and that was one of the misunderstandings we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To save time, I don't want to go through all the documents contained in these two binders, but let me ask you: Can we find in either of them any document reflecting that our side did not comply with its obligations or that something was not consistent with our agreement with the OSCE? Because KVM conducted many inspections. Did they find during their inspections of our weaponry anything that was inconsistent with the agreement concerning weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, they did not find any cases of non-compliance. For instance, until the 27th, at 1200 hours, the Pristina Corps was under obligation to withdraw -- to withdraw all its forces in the spirit of the agreement, and before the Kosovo Verification Mission arrived, their job was done by the KDOM, which was a diplomatic mission formed jointly by many embassies. And in the month of November, they covered all our units to the maximum - all barracks, all the units deployed - and they determined that we had fully complied with the agreement. And we continued to comply with that agreement until the termination of the mandate of the mission. And even when we undertook certain measures, we were entitled to do so in terms of security of our units and the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the KVM withdrawn from the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: It was withdrawn on the 20th of March, 1999, in order for the bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to begin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, regarding their conduct towards the KLA - you mentioned it briefly - what was the condition of the KLA before the arrival of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, that was an organisation that was completely broken, crushed. In end September it did no longer represent a force. They had limited territories under their control. All communications, all the roads were free for traffic. And on the 29th of September, we analysed all the operations we had undertaken against terrorist groups, and we had established that they were completely successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, what was their situation, the situation of the KLA after the arrival of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, they began to be revived a little, to return to the areas they had held before they were crushed, and even conquer new areas that they had not held. Before 1998, they began to recruit new troops, to conduct more intensive training, to organise themselves better. In logistical terms, it advanced and even obtained some anti-aircraft weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the attitude of the mission to such developments within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The view of the mission was completely benevolent, especially since they had a standing representative in the staff of the KLA and they were completely aware of everything that was going on, but they didn't take any steps to stop it. However, in cases where we had to react to such developments, they would say, "Please don't. This would irritate them. Withdraw," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the victims of KLA attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Primarily their unloyal citizens whom they deemed to be insufficiently patriotic. Secondly, Serbs, who were kidnapped. Also the police and the army. Everything that represented the state and the state authorities in Kosovo and Metohija was a target of attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did equipment for the KLA arrive from, and where did KLA members go for training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: They got most of their weapons in 1997. After the break-up of state authorities in the Republic of Albania and after mass robberies of their arms depots, the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army armed itself well. Other routes for smuggling weapons went through Albania towards Kosovo. We managed to intercept trailers coming from Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did our side - because you led our team - did our side inform the KVM of all important events and incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: We reported to the mission on a daily basis about all important events on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. We had a regular compulsory daily contact at 1000 hours, but we also had many other contacts during the day, and we reported all important things to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that one of the points of the agreement to -- one of the points of the agreement was to reduce our forces to the level required. How was that determined, that level?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, through KDOM there was a diplomatic mission that was formed by embassies of the US, France, Canada, and other countries. That KDOM later blended with the Verification Mission in Kosovo and Metohija. Only one segment of the KDOM, the American segment, did not blend with the mission. They verified the previous stage or, rather, our compliance at the previous stage, and all other components of the KDOM apart from the American one blended with the KVM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they established that there was no integration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any misunderstandings with the KVM mission concerning exits and movements of our troops from barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: We were under obligation to report all movements the size of a company and upwards, everything that came into Kosovo or left Kosovo, and we reported all that ourselves. And all misunderstandings and problems that occurred occurred in December when we received a new batch of young soldiers in December, and we had to train them because we cannot -- we could not train them within the barracks. And you have to know that our army does not consist of professional soldiers but of conscripts. So every time our troops left the barracks for training caused a problem with the Verification Mission, although in prior negotiations they had said, "Yes, we understand that you have to train your soldiers, but you are irritating the KLA, they will attack, you will return fire, and there will be a conflict." That was the reaction of the mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about our security forces? I mean both the army and the police. Did they react to provocation or would they be the first to provoke and attack the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, if you took those daily reports and looked at them, you would see that the army or the police of Yugoslavia never caused a problem. They never fired first. They only undertook such action as was necessary to protect their forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, what was the approach of the authorities - I mean not only the army and the police but also the state authorities - towards the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: There was no discrimination. The Albanian population was treated equally with the other population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tabs 16 to 19, you have reports on the cooperation with the mission for October 1998. Can we find in these reports any incidents wherein our side did not comply with its obligations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't think we have to go document-by-document because that would take a lot of time. These reports are daily, weekly, and regular reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we take one regular weekly report written on the 29th October, 1998, and it was written by the head of the liaison team from the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is tab number 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 17, 17. These reports always followed a uniform pattern. Item 1 was always movements by units of company strength and above. That sort of thing was reported daily to the OSCE mission. I don't want to read it here, but you can see it in every report. Item 2 of such report would deal with incidents involving members of army units and measures undertaken against the members of the VJ involved in the incidents, as well as observations on activities by the OSCE missions and its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the headings of these three items that were reflected in every report; movements, incidents, and observations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, along with other activities. But these would be the three main points that would be listed in every report and reported daily -- both on a daily and weekly basis. You can see -- in fact, I'm not going to read item 1, I'm going to read item 3. "On the 27th of October, in the barracks in Urosevac, a diplomatic-military mission visited. The team visited areas where the MC-243 had been deployed; Stimlje, Dulje, and Birac. And the mission did not have any objections. Also, representatives of another KDOM mission toured other areas - Dulje, Doganovici, Grncar - also without any remarks or comments." This reflects the conduct of our forces and the fact that they were reduced to the levels of February 1998. On the 27th, the mission visited Kosovski Junaci barracks and had no particular remarks. On the 28th, we also see that one team visited, consisting of three US officers. They visited barracks in Djakovica, and since they were unannounced, they did not have authorisation to inspect the barracks. You can see that from 9.30 to 1200 hours the same team visited the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade and inspected the artillery weapons in the Vranje garrison in compliance with the Dayton agreement. They also had no objections to our compliance. It was stipulated strictly how much artillery and other offensive weaponry every barracks was allowed to have, and we had to report to the office in Vienna the exact deployment of our forces and equipment. If a piece of equipment was being repaired, we had to report that to the office in Vienna, as well as the date when it was returned to the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, during these inspections, was there a single irregularity that was found during the entire tenure of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, not a single irregularity, although you can see on page 3 in paragraph 1 that a team inspected combat equipment in Vucitrn barracks, and that starting at 8.40, ending with 10.40 hours, the same team checked the combat equipment in Kosovska Mitrovica garrison. The team had an exact map and details of the deployment of the 125th Motorised Brigade and strategic war reserves in the brigade's zone of responsibility. They also had information about the organisation and establishment structure and numerical strength of the brigade's combat equipment. This was no exception. They had all this information about every unit of the army of Yugoslavia. There was no problem in inspection. And after such a complete inspection and preparation, they did not have any remarks or objections to the way we were complying with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, you have here in tabs 19 to 39 once again reports which relate to November. Are they all your own reports in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, they are. This is a team or, rather, this was a report written by the team of the 3rd Army, but not single point written by them here were they able to write unless they received it from me. So it was a team from the Pristina Corps that wrote these reports, but they were a sort of service which sent it on to the General Staff in order to comply. At the beginning we tried to comply that chain of command, upwards and downwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now from, 19 to 39, tabs 19 to 39, we have -- they all contain reports written in November 1998. Do we need to dwell on any one of them as being characteristic, a characteristic event, or are they reports which confirm the regularity on the part -- of conduct on the part of our side, or irregularities perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, you're not going to find any irregularities on our part in these reports. All the reports merely confirm the things we did and how we complied with the agreements that we were duty-bound to do. So in these reports you will see that controls had already started within the border belt in the units on the territory, and we lodged a protest with the SMIP in Pristina and requested that this should not be done in that way but that this should be announced in advantages, as stipulated by the agreement, because they were unannounced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in these unannounced visits, were they able to establish any irregularities on our part at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No. There were no irregularities. The only thing was that they weren't able to enter the border belt and control the units. All they would say was, "You're not announced. We haven't received announcements from the liaison officer, so go to the garrison, contact the liaison officer, and once he grants you permission, you'll be able to visit."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why was this insisted upon? Why did they have to contact the liaison officer? Of course, there's the general explanation why a liaison officer exists at all in the first place, but why was strict adherence to this required?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, we never knew who could enter. Anybody could take an OSCE vehicle and enter and say they were verifiers and enter the border belt. They could say, "I want to control the area, to check out the area." So soldiers on the ground didn't know who the verifiers were. They didn't know who their leaders were. They were just regular soldiers doing their military service. They weren't professional soldiers, they were civilians trained for a period of five months, plus an extra period of four months in which they did their military service, so they weren't well-versed in affairs of that kind. They couldn't determine themselves or make decisions themselves and check and verify to see whether they were actual members of the Verification Mission or whether anybody had taken the car over, put on a badge, and come to control them. So that was something that was not allowed. And in fact I don't know any other place where this would have been allowed without authorisation and permission and control, without you being held by someone there and said, "There you have it, go ahead." And if there were any misunderstandings, then somebody would have to mediate, and that was the liaison officer. He was best placed, he knew what had to be done and had the authorisation and power to do things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were your units informed that in any situation the mission would be -- or members of the mission would be escorted by a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That's the information that they received, that's what they had been prepared for, and so they saw that these conditions were complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a given situation. They came to a barracks. There would be a guard on duty, a soldier on duty in front of the barracks. Now, did that soldier have any information about the Verification Mission and how to behave towards members of the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The soldier on duty was there to guard the barracks. He was -- if he didn't -- he didn't have any information about who he was to let through or not, and foreigners could not be allowed to explain that to him. For example, when General Drewienkiewicz arrived, he started to apply this kind of method: He arrived at the barracks and said, "I want to go into the barracks and conduct an inspection." "Now, who gave you permission to do so?" He would say, "I have the right to do so, and I wish to do so." Now, the guard would not let him in, and then the officer on duty would have to react. He didn't know what it was all about. And then he would park his vehicle in Pristina at the entrance to the barracks and wouldn't leave for 15 minutes. So the officer on duty said, "Would you please move your vehicle because there's a problem with entrance into the barrack." And he would say, "There's no sign saying that." And then he would have a cup of coffee and keep his vehicle parked in front of the entrance to the barracks. Later on this would happen in Prizren. He would film the barracks, he would say, "I want to conduct an inspection in the barracks." The barracks would see what they -- what he wants, and they would say, "Well, I don't have permission, authorisation to let you in." The Dayton Accord specifically stated who was in charge and who was allowed to do what and issue what authorisation, permission. So authorisation and permission would be granted for the border belt and not the facilities and barracks, equipment, and materiel, and so on and so forth, control of the units. So this would not be allowed. No control and inspection within the barracks. Although this was up to the brigade command. So this kind of conduct, which was very problematic, wouldn't be allowed. The soldier knew -- on duty knew he wasn't able to allow anybody to enter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he could allow somebody to enter if he had permission from his superior officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any problems when there were regular procedures, when the liaison officer was present and inspection had to take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Never. When the liaison officer was present, you could always enter all the border belts, all the units on the territory, but just not into the barracks because, pursuant to the agreement, they did not have the right to inspect units within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, let's have a look at tabs 40 to 48. Once again, they are all reports relating to the month of December. Now, in those reports can we find any irregularities anywhere, or perhaps - how shall I put this? - any problems that might have occurred which our organs would were not able to settle in cooperation with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This tab verifies events taking place in December. From the 1st of December to the end of December. In these daily reports, from tab 40, it says, for example, under point 2, Incidents, it says: "On the 1st of December, at about 1000 hours, in the sector of the combat group 549/4 in the village of Zjum, an OSCE mission jeep with licence plates stopped and two persons came out. They videotaped the disposition of the Combat Group's tanks. They stayed ten minutes and then set off in the direction of Dragas." Filming wasn't allowed of the units on the territory and in the barracks, which is what they did on that particular day. Now, on the 1st of December, a contact between the OSCE mission and the liaison officer of the 53rd Border Battalion, which had been arranged so that the incident that had taken place at the Likane border post on the 28th of November, 1999, could be verified, was not established. The contact did not take place. I think that this -- at this incident at the Likane border post somebody was killed who tried to enter Kosovo and Metohija from Albania. A terrorist attempt. A terrorist attempted to enter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are your daily reports and weekly reports; is that right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do they contain information about what actually happened with respect to the subject matter you're explaining to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes. They contain all the information on the subjects I went into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we find any irregularities there on our side and how they cooperated with the OSCE, with the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, we have here a large number of daily reports which have already been tendered as exhibits during General Delic's testimony, and they are reports which relate to 1999 alone. And they're numbered -- they have been assigned numbers because they're not new tabs. Now, in these reports -- and I'm mentioning them here because they are your own documents and they were tendered and admitted when General Delic testified. Now these reports 1 to 30, do they contain anything which could represent any form of irregularity at all vis-a-vis the Verification Mission or obligations taken on by our side at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: As for these reports, all we can say is that from them we can see our relationship and attitude towards the verifiers, what the verifiers' attitude was towards us and towards certain events. Perhaps -- or, rather, there were different interpretations of certain events, but no irregularities on our part were visible here in these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that relates to January. Now, in 31 to 51, tabs 31 to 51, we have the February reports that were also presented during General Delic's testimony. They are also your reports, are they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in those reports and for that period of time and taking them all together, could you point out any deviations at all or incompatibilities between our -- the conduct on the part of our organs and what was stipulated in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I would just like to indicate one problem that took place. The greatest problem of deviation from that, not on our part but it was the Verification Mission, was when the event of Racak took place. We had an agreement with the verifiers by which if any incident should break out or any event should take place, that they should not -- nobody should go public until the facts of the matter had been established beforehand. Now, for the first time the verifiers were very blatant in their actions. Without previously checking out the situation, they went to the media, informed them about Racak, about an alleged massacre against innocent civilians having been conducted and perpetrated by the forces of the MUP and army of Yugoslavia. And you could find something relating to that in the January reports and our contacts with them in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm a little concerned about the exhibit position. I've got a schedule provided by the accused, and so far as I can see, 31 to 51 are not 1999 documents. Maybe I've got a different document than any document the Court has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he has a separate list for those that have been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may well be, but if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was looking for it but I couldn't find.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he is assuming that we are on notice as to the documents he's going to be speaking about and we would have retrieved them in some way and considered them, the answer is at the moment we haven't done that because, unless we've missed the document, we haven't been on notice to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also as for documents which would refer to the events in December 1998, although the transcript says that it's from tab 40 to 48, I would assume it should be from tab 40 to tab 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what do you have to say about these administrative matters?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm talking about documents now that were presented during the testimony of General Delic, and they were just assigned numbers and were not put into tabs because they had already been tendered into evidence as exhibits. So we have documents, a set of documents for January, from the 1st of January until the 31st of January, and those are the numbers 1 to 31. Then we have documents for February also introduced during the testimony of General Delic. And finally, the documents for March with numbers which relate to the Verification Mission until it left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At least you should identify the numbers in order for the Chamber to look at those documents later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, I'll tell you straight away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we don't have that copy of that document at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. From 1 to 30. 1 is D300, tab 262, and you have that in the list. Number 2, which was provided during the testimony of General Delic, is Exhibit 300, tab 263, and so on. Number 3 is D300, tab 264, and onwards in that same order. So you have each of these exhibits identified and tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you're referring to. That's not before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, then that is my mistake, but I'm telling you what they're about. So I'm referring to documents 1 to 31. All of them come under D300, ranging from numbers two hundred and -- number 1 is 262, number 2 is 263, and so on and so forth until number 31. All that comes under D300. And the same refers and applies to the other group of documents, documents that have been marked for identification and presented here during General Delic's testimony. May I be allowed to continue now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: D300, 262 to 292 have been previously admitted, we think, from our records as we've just looked at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He doesn't have to spend time for what has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. I think that's where the confusion arises in calling it 1 to 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, submit what you have to the Registry so that we can have copies made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall do that, Mr. Robinson. But as I say, as the documents have been admitted, I'm just going through them because we have here testimony by the author of the documents themselves, and he is here to indicate their main characteristics, taking them always a collective body of documents. And if there are any incidents, then he is here to draw our attention to them. That is why I'm not going into them in detail, because we've already been through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I should now like to dwell on just one matter, Colonel, something that you raised when you said that there were problems with respect to the incident in Racak. And in the meantime I have received -- or, rather, I was found the document by Professor Rakic amongst these other documents that Mr. Nice's service had at their disposal. Since I haven't had the time to make copies of this document, I hope that it has already -- or they have already been introduced into evidence. And what we're looking at now is a document dated the 16th of January, 1999, the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the group for cooperation with the OSCE mission, and it is a conversation between General Dusan Loncar, leader of the coordination team of the federal government for Kosovo and Metohija, with General Drewienkiewicz, the deputy head of OSCE mission. Do you have that document with you? We handed over the document, on the last day, albeit, but we did hand it over during the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, since this is a record of that meeting between General Loncar and General Drewienkiewicz --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number of that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't know. 39130 are the last numbers, and then there is one that's erased. Maybe it's number 1. It says Exhibit, but it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suspect it may be Exhibit 94, tab 28. And if the Chamber has brought its file of Racak documents, if I'm right about that it will be number 11. I'll check to see if it is number 11, and if my copy is unmarked, I can make it available for the overhead projector. Yes, that would appear to be the document. Providing I can have it back, I can lay this one on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, please. There is one mark but it's irrelevant. It's a highlight is all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the English text now on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by the first words, it should be identical. I'm not going to dwell on the first page. Colonel, could you please take a look at the second page of the document. On the second page, third paragraph. The third paragraph. It says: "General Drewienkiewicz next demanded from General Loncar that the Stimlje operation be dealt with. That is the main reason why he came." Could you read on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that it's not on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we find the correct place in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. That's about Decani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Decani. It's Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Mr. Nort hands it to me, I'll try and find it. Thank you very much. Well, Your Honours, it should be -- it should be the passage I think we've been looking at where there is reference to Decani, because by my calculation -- okay. Found it. Thank you to Ms. Dicklich.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is no mention of Decani over here, but never mind. I assume it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Decani is on the document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the middle of the screen we can see "Stimlje."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read this paragraph, please. "He said that he had --"

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: "He said that he had information indicating that over 30 civilians were killed there, among them a large number of 8-year-old children, women and elderly. He informed General Loncar that both he and Walker, along with a large number of journalists, would go to the scene as soon as the meeting was over and that they would inform the OSCE, the international community, about all of this. He threatened or, rather, he warned that this would be 'very bad for our side.'"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause there. Do you know about what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at that meeting during that conversation, but I just want to say that General Drewienkiewicz called me as early as the 15th, on the evening of the 15th, around 2300 hours, 2330 hours; it was almost midnight. He phoned me, and he asked me about the action in Racak. I explained to him that what I knew was that this was an anti-terrorist action carried out by the MUP. He said then that his first information was that there were a few dead, five or six dead, and the same number of wounded persons, but he did not talk to me about women, children, et cetera. So that's the evening of the 15th. The next day, in the morning, I maintained communication with him from my office, which was at the Federal Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija, and General Loncar's office was right next to mine. He told me, "You committed a massacre in Racak. You killed women and children. Walker and I are going there with journalists in order to disclose this to the world." I asked him not to act abruptly. Let us all stick to our agreement. The investigation authorities should investigate the matter, with the participation of the Kosovo Verification Mission, and then when we see how things stand, then we could come out in public. He replied to me then that Mr. Walker had already left for Racak with journalists and that he was already there. He requested a meeting with General Loncar. We agreed on that meeting. We scheduled it. As far as I can remember, around midday, 11.30. It wasn't midday yet, but say around 11.30. General Drewienkiewicz, when this meeting took place - this is the record of that meeting - the record was made by a person from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I see the signature here Radenko Simic, whereas the information note itself was signed by Mr. Slana, who was head of the foreign ministry office there. What General Drewienkiewicz said was fully described, and I've already read out this paragraph to you, that over 30 civilians were killed there, whereas the largest number of these civilians were 8-year-old children, women, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, there is something illogical here now. He says that he told General Loncar that Walker and he, with a large number of journalists, immediately at the end of this meeting would go to the scene, whereas you say that as he was scheduling this meeting in the telephone conversation with you, he said that Walker had already set out and that he was on his way to the scene. So these two do not match. What's it all about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: What he said here does not correspond to that but the truth is what I stated a few moments ago. During the telephone conversation, I was told that he and Walker would go there with journalists, and when I told him they should wait, he told me that Walker had already left. When he came to the meeting, he said that he and Walker would go after this meeting, that they would go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The truth was that Walker was already there. This meeting went on for about an hour or an hour and a half, so we ended it about 1300 hours, whereas Walker, on the 16th, by 1300 hours was already there with some KLA commanders, talking to them. He was in Racak. That is the information we had. And it's illogical that at 1300 hours Walker could have been in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This can easily be established on the basis of his movements on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please now look at the bottom of the second page, the last paragraph -- or, rather, the one but last. It's a biggish paragraph. This is a record of what General Loncar said. Could you please read out what it says. "Further on, he pointed out that in all movements of the army and the MUP --" what does it say here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one but last paragraph on page 2. "Loncar expresses protest because of General Drewienkiewicz's statement."

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: "Loncar expressed protest over General Drewienkiewicz's statement that he did not know who shot first, emphasising that this is highly unfair."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just pause there. What's this all about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, near Rznic, two verifiers were wounded. And on the 16th of January, a motor vehicle from Regional Centre 1 - that's Prizren - was shot at. There was a bullet that was fired at it. The so-called Kosovo Liberation Army intentionally shot at the verifiers, and that proved to be true later on. We knew that straight away. When we first met, that's what he said, because Mr. Ciaglinski, he said it. He knew about it because it was one of his verifiers that was in the vehicle and who was wounded, and he knew exactly who shot at him. That's what I said at the very outset. The problem was whenever there was an incident, especially when General Drewienkiewicz was concerned, he always suspected our side of having done something and we always had to prove that we didn't do it. The KLA commanders themselves admitted they did that. That's what Mr. Ciaglinski stated too. Their assessment was that this was done intentionally, on purpose, because the KLA commander for Jablanica noted that they should not follow police and army vehicles, especially in areas that were under their control. And I can tell you that from the 15th of January onwards, verifiers teams were no longer following the movements of the army and the MUP when they went through the territory that was the control under the -- under the control of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, and that's why Mr. Loncar said to Drewienkiewicz that what he said was unfair, because it is known very well who shot at the verifiers and why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Drewienkiewicz's reaction to Loncar's protest over the fact that he said that he did not know although it was known that the members of the KLA did it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, he did not react. He stuck to what he said originally, and especially at this meeting. He was very angry. He came very angry and aggressive. And it says here in the record that he didn't even want to have a cup of coffee. And that is the polite way to behave in our parts, to have a cup of coffee when you first meet up. He didn't want to have coffee with us because he was so angry over what had happened in Racak. That is what he stated. Later on, he calmed down a bit. Towards the end he wasn't that arrogant, but he stuck to his original position, although later on that proved to be the wrong position and incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it say further on? What does Loncar say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: He pointed out that, as they had told him earlier on, the action was carried out in order to apprehend the terrorists who had killed a policeman, and since they encountered well-prepared resistance, well prepared by the terrorists, he pointed out that they had been informed about our intentions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the sentence that you omitted? "He further pointed out --" You did not read that. What was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: "He pointed out further that the KVM was informed about all movements of Yugoslavia army and MUP units and that this was the case relating to operations -- activities, rather, around Stimlje."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can be seen on the basis of what Loncar is saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: What can be seen here and also on the basis of our reports was that we reported daily on what was going on, and that also pertains to the Stimlje action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Loncar pointed out that you always informed them in a timely fashion and that they were informed about the operation or action in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes. The MUP informed the KVM that they would have an action in Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Drewienkiewicz react to that in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, he did not react. He simply kept silent. He presented what he had to say, and he did not react to what General Loncar said to him. He just pursued what he had to say, and he always stuck to what he had to say at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As head of the liaison team, did you know that they had been informed about this event in Racak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I knew about that through Loncar because I was Loncar's deputy, the deputy and assistant at the federal office for liaising with the Verification Mission Kosovo and Metohija. I was leader of the team on behalf of the Pristina Corps, but also at the same time I was Loncar's deputy. So I know about what Loncar was saying in terms of the MUP activity, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm just going to ask you to comment on yet another record that I have here that we got recently -- or, rather, on the last day. That is a record of the meeting between Aleksandar Nikolaev, head of the political department, from the 12th of January. So it's just a few days before this, just a few days before what happened in Racak, that is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I've just found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number is 139112. The Foreign Ministry office in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're not immediately sure whether this has been exhibited. If the accused wants to produce documents, even if they've been provided to him under Rule 68 or otherwise, it remains his duty to make them available to us in one way or another. I'm doing my best to make good his shortcomings, but on this document I'm not sure that we've got a document to hand. It doesn't appear to be in the Racak list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the position? Where is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says "Exhibit," there is an empty space. And it is obviously coming from the office of Mr. Nice, because I have no other documents in this connection. It has an ERN number, 0139112, and it's a record of consultations with Mr. Aleksandar Nikolaev from the KVM. If you agree, we can put it on the ELMO, and the witness and I will have it in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Colonel, put it on the ELMO, and you can read from there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Which page do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Dicklich's search would suggest from the ERN number given that this may be Exhibit 792, tab 4. We'll try and find a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will skip the part where it says that the meeting was held on the premises of the office. Look at point 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Shall I read?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's a meeting with Aleksandar Nikolaev, chief reconstruction political internal department, KVM. "Our collocutor presented us with some details regarding events in the KVM following the murder of policemen and kidnapping of VJ members."

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "Immediately upon receiving the news of the said events, General Drewienkiewicz informed Walker in Washington. Ambassador Walker asked General Drewienkiewicz to wait a little before sending the report to Washington, warning him," in quotation marks, "that is possibly disinformation. Despite that, General Drewienkiewicz organised a meeting with other deputies of Walker and they decided by majority vote to send the report to Washington nevertheless, over which Walker was furious," in quotation marks. "Furthermore, during this meeting the collocutor informed us with their assessment of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija made by the analysis department of the KVM on the 9th of January, consisting of the intelligence service of the KVM, and so on. This department includes American, English, and German officers, analysts. This assessment covers current situation and intentions of the KLA, VJ, MUP, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does he say about KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: He says: "It is assessed that the KLA shall intensify their activities in the area of Mitrovica, Urosevac, as well as on the Urosevac-Suva Reka-Stimlje route."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's this part around Racak.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: "This assessment is corroborated by the latest activities of the KLA (murder of policemen and kidnapping of soldiers.) It is our estimate that these two actions were coordinated very well, even professionally, in an organised way, and implemented in the same fashion. The KLA announces new attacks against MUP members. It is obvious that the KLA is trying to reduce all contacts with the KVM to official ones, and it is done through so-called public relations officers, wherein Rusti Asari [phoen] is the representative of the KLA."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say further on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: "Assert -- it is evident that there is a gradual distancing," in quotation marks, "of the KLA from the population, and attempts to establish on the territory held by the KLA other parallel authorities such as MUP, municipal organs, et cetera. The KVM is increasingly depicted as incompetent, and this trend in the information produced by the KLA is evermore pronounced. It is expected that it will continue. It is also expected that they will fabricate incidents, even murders of Albanians, to be ascribed to the MUP and the VJ. "The KLA is taking actions to intimidate the population. VJ was expected to react much more strongly after the kidnapping of soldiers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say about the VJ? --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are going too fast with this on-site translation. Can we return the previous page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and the witness, the interpreter says you're going too fast. Bear in mind that she's seeing the document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you give me that exhibit number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 792, tab 4. While I'm on my feet, we are trying to get English version down here as soon as possible because it really is very difficult to follow this without an English version to read. The accused, may I invite him through the Court, must recognise his duty is to get these documents available in advance. He should be able to track down, from the documents he's got, whether they are exhibits, but he knows that if, in the final analysis, he's unable to do that himself or through the pro se liaison office or through my learned friends Mr. Kay, he can always ask Ms. Dicklich to help in advance and she will do so, although it takes time away from her other exercises, her other jobs. And it would help us all if this is done so we can have documents in advance. Now we finally have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. The remarks are very pertinent, Mr. Milosevic, and in future if you come here unprepared, I will do what would be done in my country: You will not be allowed to lead evidence relating to that document. You must come here fully prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the issue where I got the document from, I have already said that I obtained it, without any doubt, from the office of Mr. Nice. It was part of the disclosure under Rule 68, part of his obligation to disclose it to me. I didn't have time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has nothing at all to do with your leading evidence from that document which you got from Mr. Nice. You must come to court prepared. You must have the copies ready for the Bench and for the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
