utterances.text: To complete the picture, in fact, it was produced through Ivasov by the Prosecution, and so the accused should be alert to the fact that he has it two different ways, and where he has it in both the form of 68 material and as an exhibit, he should of course alert us to the fact that it's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Colonel, this is a document reflecting a conversation on the 12th of January, that is three days prior to the events in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's an analysis made by the intelligence department of the Kosovo Verification Mission, and they expect fabrication of incidents by the KLA, even murders of Albanians, to be ascribed to the MUP and the army of Yugoslavia. So that's the expectation, the forecast, of the Verification Mission. Is that written in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are Urosevac and the area around Racak --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Stimlje and Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- mentioned twice in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't dwell on it any further, because I had a couple of more documents to which Mr. Nice might have the same objection. I will not proceed with them in view of the way you reacted, Mr. Robinson, saying that I can not lead such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to your reports. Tell me, under the numbers 31 to 51, can we find documents relating to testimony of General Delic? Are they your documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 31 is D300, tab 301. 32 is D300, tab 302, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have now these documents from our collection down here so that they can be placed on the overhead projector, just us doing for the accused that which he should have done for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On behalf of the accused, I thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, it's not only disrespectful, it's inefficient, because we waste a lot of time trying to find these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Mr. Robinson, that documents that have already been admitted into evidence may be led as long as I mention the number of the exhibit, that I don't have to produce them again because they are already part the evidence. I'm just asking the witness, who authored these documents, to testify, to speak to their contents and their authenticity. They were produced during the testimony of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, even if they're already exhibits, you should have copies for us in court, because we don't have all the exhibits here. But deal with this briefly. Or, as Judge Kwon is just saying to me, you may inform us beforehand so we can have the copies brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, in this entire overview of documents for the month of February, do you have any incident reflected wherein it could be said that our side had not honoured its obligations towards the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Our side honoured all its obligations towards the Verification Mission, except in those cases where the Verification Mission was not acting in the spirit of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any specific event for the month of February reflected in these documents where we can see an omission on our side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I could not find any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And finally, this overview of documents also contains the numbers from 52 to 73 that were also produced through General Delic relating to the month of March. 52 is D300, tab 448. 53 is D300, 449, and so on. Daily and weekly reports. Do weekly reports cover, for the most part, all that is contained in daily reports only in summary form? Are they consistent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: They are completely consistent. And the summary reports summarise the information for the previous week's -- for the previous week reflected in daily reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this batch of documents for March, do we see any incident wherein our side did not act consistently with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, there are no such incidents. I would just like to say that there is an incident where -- a case where the Pristina Corps command made an assessment that their position was unfavourable and that the KLA had 6.000 to 7.000 men in the north of Albania, 2 to 3.000 in Macedonia, and around 15.000 men under arms in Kosovo and Metohija. That was the equivalent to 20 to 25.000 armed combatants; that is, terrorists. In that period we had around four to five daily attacks against civilians and the police. Out of all the districts in Kosovo and Metohija, four were completely overwhelmed by terrorist activity. Out of 28 municipalities, 19 were the site of some sort of combat activity, and 300 civilians -- and 300 villages were held by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the report for a period during -- or, rather, just after the arrival of the KVM. Did you compare the situation with violence at the beginning of KVM tenure and at the end?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I already said that this is the situation when the KVM was leaving, and I already said that before they arrived the KLA was completely crushed. They were not an organised force. They were under-equipped, and they did not hold many territories under their control. I had just begun to say what the assessment of the Pristina Corps was at the beginning of March when the -- some units were already arriving as reinforcements to the Pristina Corps because its strength was under the establishment level, but we had informed the Verification Mission that we would be doing that. It was a time when many aircraft had already been deployed in Italy vis-a-vis Yugoslavia, and we notified the Verification Mission that without these reinforcements we would be unable to deal and successfully perform our duties. It could be treated as a violation of the agreement between our country and the OSCE, because we were supposed to reduce our strength to the level of February 1998, but we were taking this step in the circumstances that I described, and I believe the signatories of the agreement were Generals Clark and Naumann, and General Djordjevic on our side. And according to that agreement, we reserved the right to bring in more forces if that was justified by a particular assessment, provided we notified the Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I hope that this -- the fact that we went through these reports very briefly is sufficient for them to be tendered into evidence. Of course there I don't mean the ones that have already been admitted into evidence during General Delic's testimony, but the other ones that range to the end of 1998, and all of them are documents of Colonel Kotur's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you identify them, Mr. Milosevic, those that have not already been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you able to help us with whether December 1998 documents have already been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It looks to me like they should have been admitted, so we're trying to track through the records to see what the rulings have been on these particular documents. We can't help you instantly, I'm sorry, Your Honour, but we're just checking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give me a minute and I'll check. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Milosevic, and we'll come back to this question. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A preliminary reckoning by Ms. Dicklich would suggest that on the list we've now been provided with, which is the exhibits to be used with Milan Kotur, on that list where it says documents have not been admitted, they have not yet been admitted because with Delic the accused did not deal with those exhibits at all, those potential exhibits. They were in the Delic file, but it may be these simply weren't touched on by him at all. Ms. Dicklich is trying to confirm the position, but it may well be that this list now provided by the accused is accurate as to the status of those documents. But I know what problems develop when there is any uncertainty about exhibits, problems that then require a great deal of work by all organs of the Tribunal working for the Court, and can I suggest that we perhaps put this back until after the next break so that we can be reasonably confident on what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, tab 2's 162 to 291 were all admitted under Delic exhibit, except for those which were marked for identification pending translations, but I haven't checked all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll follow the course suggested by Mr. Nice. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apology. I'll check it. We'll check it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you asked me to identify them. I have already identified them. I identified them when I asked the witness my question. But let me repeat: In tabs 19 to 39 we have reports from the Verification Mission dating back to November 1998, so that is dealing with the month of November. And I asked the witness questions about that set of documents. Now, in tabs 40 to 68, you have reports about the Verification Mission dating to December, and I also asked the witness questions with respect to that set of documents. So I have complied with your request and ask that these tabs be tendered, tabs 19 to 39 and 40 to 68 inclusive. And then afterwards, we have the Delic documents that are incorporated by number identification and not tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The registrar has confirmed that they were not previously admitted, so we will admit them. Yes, assign an exhibit number for the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And please could you admit the previous tabs that the witness dealt with individually; the diagram, the map regarding the organisation, and everything else referring to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the Verification Mission, the ones I explained.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was provided by Mr. Milosevic will be Exhibit D332.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they are admitted. Do you have numbers for the -- the same binder, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, we heard testimony here from General Maisonneuve. Did you have an opportunity of meeting General Maisonneuve; and if so, what were his positions within the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet General Maisonneuve. He was at the head of the Regional Centre, Regional Centre number 1, in fact, in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to his testimony here, I should like to ask you a few questions, and I consider that you are well placed to give answers to them. He said that after the incident in Racak, the command of the brigade in Urosevac, General Krsman Jelic, did not wish to meet with him. Maisonneuve claims that he managed to have a meeting with General Jelic only three weeks later, when he managed to force you to persuade Jelic to have the meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, as far as you gentlemen are concerned, that is on page 5821 of the transcript, and the date of the testimony was the 29th of May, 2002. And if need be, I can quote from the transcript that particular page, but I've already given you a summary and precis of what it says there and I'd like to hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maisonneuve, well, I'm surprised that he made a statement to that effect, because as a general of the Canadian army he could have known, and I think he did know, the kind of relationships that prevail in all armies throughout the world, including the army of Yugoslavia. First and foremost, I was not the person who was superior to General Delic for me to be able to persuade him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Ah, right, General Krsman Jelic, that's right. For me to be able to persuade him to come to a meeting. I was just head of the team liaising with the Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, let's not say forced, but did you try and persuade him to talk to Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No. The moment the request came in via the mission's staff in Pristina, headquarters in Pristina, to the effect that General Maisonneuve would like to have a meeting with General Delic, we organised it straight away. And his previous attempts to hold a meeting with Delic, whether he wanted to or not, I wasn't informed of that. But at that moment, that was the line of communication: It went from the Regional Centre with the centre in Pristina and then the headquarters in Pristina, links with the Pristina Corps that I headed and that Mr. Maisonneuve could have contacted only the liaison officer or, rather, General Delic's liaison officer at the Urosevac garrison, with the proviso that General Maisonneuve did not cover that particular area himself. It was an area and territory under the supervision of the Regional Centre 5 from Pristina. Now, why Mr. Maisonneuve wanted to have that meeting, what the reasons were for that is no longer important, because all the obligations taken over by the 243rd Mechanised Brigade from Urosevac to be fulfilled vis-a-vis the mission, it did so via the liaison officer. The same thing that applied to the Pristina Corps, the -- through the liaison team headed by me. So that relationships between us and the commanders and Delic and so forth does not stand. There was no need for me to persuade anyone to do anything in the way described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, generally speaking, did General Jelic avoid meeting General Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, Delic never avoided a meeting with Maisonneuve but quite simply Delic did not always have the time to meet him when Maisonneuve took it into his head to have a meeting with the commander. That's why you need liaison officers. And they were best placed to organise anything that needed to be done, to convey anything that needed to be conveyed, and so on and so forth. Now, I myself, having said that, can claim with full responsibility because I was a brigade commander for a long time, and the brigade was deployed over a distance of 40 kilometres during a period of intensive action on the part of the so-called Liberation Army of Kosovo, attacking the brigade and the whole territory, so Delic [as interpreted] did not have time to have a meeting, if he wanted a meeting, scheduled for the same day. You would have to make your request in advance, and I always ensured this through the corps and this would be made possible the next day, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned liaison officers. Now tell me this: Were the liaison officers always at the disposal of the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the brigade commander wasn't always available but the -- his liaison officer was, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. I was available 24 hours, that is to say round the clock, in Pristina, at the headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, in previous answer the transcript should say Jelic instead of Delic. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're talking about Krsman Jelic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I made a slip of the tongue when I said Delic instead of saying Jelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. For the record, I'd just like to emphasise that we're talking about Krsman Jelic. Now, General Maisonneuve goes on to say the following, and we're now going on to seeing that the meeting was held, we've clarified that position, how the meeting came about in the first place, but he goes on to say the following: He says that Jelic at a meeting with him didn't wish to confirm that he had collaborated with the MUP during the operation in Racak. Maisonneuve says that General Jelic on that occasion said that his forces did not shoot at the village but at the surrounding parts, targeting two other villages. So Krsman Jelic did not confirm that the army and MUP worked in concert. And you can find that on page 5790 in the transcript of Major -- General Maisonneuve's testimony. Were you present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and it was held in Urosevac within the framework of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it exactly that General Jelic told Maisonneuve, and what was Maisonneuve's reaction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Mr. Maisonneuve insisted to know whether the army had taken part together with the MUP in the operation at Racak or not. Mr. Jelic denied it and said that the army had not taken part, that it was a MUP operation, and he expressed a certain amount of dissatisfaction and insisted that that was the case. But Jelic explained how things stood. I didn't interfere because it was up to Mr. Jelic, who was responsible for everything that went on in that area. I said very little during that meeting, but I do know that Jelic claimed that the army had not taken part, and he presented what it says in the record of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your knowledge of the situation at that time. Did the army take part or not? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: My knowledge tells me that the army did not take part. It was an anti-terrorist operation organised by the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. General Maisonneuve also stated that after the event in Racak he visited the headquarters of the staff of the 243rd Brigade in Urosevac, told them that it was his intention to receive confirmation about the participation of their troops from the commander and their responsibilities for the events in Racak. According to Maisonneuve, at that meeting, at which the commander of the brigade, Krsman Jelic, was not present, Colonel Petrovic -- now, who is Colonel Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic was a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. He was a liaison officer of the Jelic's brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Confirmed that MUP had conducted the operation in Racak but that he was supported by a Praga and a tank of the 243rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I never received a report from the liaison officer to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Colonel Petrovic said what Maisonneuve said he said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Had Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic said that, then I would have had it in the daily report from Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic, and that would have been contained in the report of the team sent to the General Staff, the team for liaisoning with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, talking of that same meeting, staying with the meeting - and in the transcript, it's on page 5766 and 67 -- 5786 and 87 of the 22nd of May, 2002, speaking about that same meeting, Maisonneuve said that he wasn't satisfied because he hadn't talked to the brigade commander but just the liaison officer by the name of Petrovic and that that than officer had told him on the occasion, and he quotes, that Stimlje was done with Pragas and armoured vehicles and one tank, on the basis of which he understood that it was support to the army of Yugoslavia. And he goes on to quote on 5788: "Stimlje was done by the MUP with Praga [In English] vehicle and one tank. And then I guess understood there that this was the VJ in support." [Interpretation] According to your knowledge and information, is this quotation by General Maisonneuve correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: There is no single officer in the 243rd Brigade, especially not a liaison officer, who would replace a small village of Racak with Stimlje. Stimlje is a municipal locality, rather large populated area, and as far as I understand it, it said that Stimlje was done with a Praga and a tank, and that has nothing to do with Racak at all. So that statement is completely incorrect, and I don't know where this comes from. There's something not right there. If Maisonneuve said that, then I don't think it can be a witness that can be believed, if anybody said that, a witness who said that. Now, Racak, Stimlje, I'm not clear what we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Stimlje is a municipal locality where the powers and authorities function normally, the police and all the organs of power and authority.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes. It is the seat of the municipality. It has a health centre, a hospital, for instance, for retarded persons. It's a rather large town, a rather large municipal town, the seat of the municipality. It's not something that could be confused with Racak or anything else like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Could any of our officers have said Stimlje was done and mean Racak, mistake that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I said that that was impossible a moment ago, especially an officer from the 243rd Mechanised Brigade in whose zone of responsibility that was anyway and he was there every day. He could not confuse Stimlje with Racak. I have my suspicions as far as that statement made by General Drewienkiewicz is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, this is General Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: General Maisonneuve, beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said that the police was involved in the action in Racak, which was obvious for them in the military because they could see them on the hill, supporting them. General Maisonneuve said in his opinion the army was supporting the MUP. That is what was confirmed to him on the meeting of the 16th of January by Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic, the liaison officer of the 243rd Brigade, with one tank and a few Pragas at least, that that was the support. This is what it says. I'm going to read it out to you: "[In English] The police had been involved in Racak. It was obvious to them. They could see them as they were up on the hill supporting, to my mind supporting the police. And at one of the meeting on the 16th with Petrovic, the liaison officer from 243rd Brigade, the lieutenant colonel, he did say that the MUP had done the operation with support of VJ with at least one tank and some Pragas." [Interpretation] So the transcript page is 5865. What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: It is true that the MUP carried out this action. However, the unit was not on a hill. It was below Canovica hill. It is in the area of the pine forest where from Racak cannot be seen. The army could not have seen it from that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could Petrovic have said anything like that at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I've already said so, just like what I said about Petrovic saying about Stimlje being done with Pragas. I doubt that Petrovic could have said this either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I was in that area. I know where the unit was located, and I know roughly what the configuration of the terrain looks like. I know that I passed there dozens of times towards Prizren. It's a very narrow road, and nothing can really be seen from the road, rather, to the south of the road where Racak is located in relation to the Stimlje-Suva Reka road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How long was that unit in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: From April 1998, I think, all of 1998, more than half a year, and then continued in 1999. So it was in that area for almost a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that unit belong to part of the units that remained, according to the agreement, at some points in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes. That unit, according to the agreement with the OSCE mission, had one of its companies in Stimlje-Suva Reka and underneath Canovica hill. Part of that unit, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was its task?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Its task was to provide security along at that road because this was a road where in 1998 for a few months -- or, rather, for a few months in 1998 we could not use that road because of the activities of the so-called KLA. And also already in 1998 we had our first casualties on that road due to the activities of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army activities. And that unit stayed there to provide security for that road or, rather, to secure safety along that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Colonel. Now I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to the testimony of General Drewienkiewicz. In part of his statement that has to do with the freeing of eight soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia that had been kidnapped by the KLA, he said that the Verification Mission members made a great effort to make it possible for these eight soldiers to be set free, those who had been captured by the KLA, and that there were many moments when they thought that the army and police would storm that position and that they were wedged between the two sides, and they were trying to calm things down. Drewienkiewicz particularly pointed out his own dedication because allegedly he slept on the floor of his office for three days in case a telephone message came. The transcript page is 2 -- 5 -- 2898. I'm not going to quote that at any length, but what do you know about the engagement of the Kosovo Verification Mission and Drewienkiewicz itself? What kind of efforts did they make in terms of setting those soldiers free?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: A few moments ago we read what the intelligence of the KVM was; namely, that we had a very lukewarm reaction to the abduction of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or, rather, that was their assessment of what our reaction was.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we read. And now this same Verification Mission that assessed our behaviour in this way is now saying that we had stormed the place. Practically an action was almost carried out and now that they were almost caught in the crossfire. I am not denying the efforts made by the gentleman who, in agreement with Mr. Sainovic, as soon as the KLA kidnapped these eight soldiers of ours they immediately asked through the Kosovo Verification Mission to establish contact with us to reach an agreement to have an exchange. We accepted that immediately. They were very satisfied with this position that we took, and Mr. Keller and Mr. Sainovic carried through this agreement on the exchange. It is true that the commander in the area of Bajgora did not always honour the agreements made. He dragged his feet. He was trying to get things done. Mr. Ciaglinski characterised him as a rather simple man, a commander who was trying to show off in front of his own soldiers and his own people. We carried out certain movements of our own units. In case the negotiations failed, we would have acted in military fashion. However, that never happened. Not even remotely was there such a situation. In these talks, when I was asked whether we were planning something like that, I said no. For as long as the talks were going on, it never crossed our minds to carry out any kind of action of this nature. So this boasting of Mr. Drewienkiewicz that they made this major effort, I really cannot see that. And as I said, their own assessment was that our reaction was rather lukewarm. This was the police, the military police, seven military policemen of the motorised brigade. There was an NCO, a crime technician, who had a Puch combat vehicle, a highly valuable one with all the equipment a crime technician uses, and also all the armour and weapons that were needed. When the KLA kidnapped soldiers, they kept all this equipment. And when they're saying that our reaction was lukewarm, they probably have in mind the fact that the soldiers were kidnapped and that this equipment was taken, because these were not ordinary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, as far as their assessment is concerned, they said that they expected a stronger reaction on the part of the military.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: We've dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've dealt with that. General Drewienkiewicz stated that on the 16th [Realtime transcript read in error "6th"] of January he had contacts with General Loncar who came to his office and said that they should talk. Loncar allegedly said to him then that he had just heard about the content of the press conference that Walker had held and that he thought that it was not done right. Loncar allegedly told me that he got instructions from Belgrade to go to Drewienkiewicz and to convey that message. Loncar, according to the witness's words, said that Walker had not indicated at the press conference that everything that happened in Racak was a response to the previous killing of the police but that the police entered Racak looking for the people who had killed policemen a week earlier, and as this witness said, Loncar tried to justify this, that is to say the presence of the armed forces of Yugoslavia in the village, before commenting on what really happened, regardless of whether this was in keeping with the orders or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please read slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must read more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is on page 2914 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whatever slip, whether of the tongue or of the transcript, the date of the 6th of January is obviously the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's the 16th. That's what I said, the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what Drewienkiewicz said on this transcript page which I've just referred to, he had contacts with Loncar who came to his office and told him that they should talk. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that contact. I believe that this -- that had this kind of contact been made, I would have known something about it. Had General Loncar gone to Drewienkiewicz's office directly without reaching previous agreement and scheduling the meeting, I really don't know anything about that. I believe that Loncar would not have gone without me or the representative of the MUP. He would not have gone to see General Drewienkiewicz on his own. He never did that before. I just know of one particular meeting. If I remember correctly, it was on the 18th, but with Mr. Walker. General --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's different.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I know what I know, that this meeting that was had around midday on the 16th, with Drewienkiewicz and myself on the premises of our office in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Drewienkiewicz says here that Loncar came to see him. And a few moments ago, just before the break, towards the end of our previous session here, we presented in the Serbian and English languages a record on the meeting held on the 16th of January - that is to same the very same day - where it says meeting between General Dusan Loncar, head of the coordination team of the federal government for Kosovo and Metohija, with General Drewienkiewicz, head of mission of the OSCE. You said that you attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a record which starts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you hear that? I'm tired of telling you. The interpreters are having difficulty following you. Read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we saw the record which unequivocally establishes that Drewienkiewicz came to the meeting where Loncar was, and the others present, those who were keeping the minutes, and you were at the meeting too. That's what you said when we were looking at the record. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what General Drewienkiewicz said during his testimony corresponds to the date mentioned here, but it does not correspond to what had allegedly happened, namely that Loncar came to see him. Here we have a record stating that he came to your office to have this meeting, and that allegedly he told him about the press conference and about the instructions from Belgrade. Was there any mention of this at the meeting where Drewienkiewicz was present together with you about any instructions from Belgrade in relation to his press conference or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, no. There were no instructions that we had, no. I think that they held this press conference only after Racak, sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I read out to you what Drewienkiewicz said. Since you were at the meeting which was held in your offices, and it says that Drewienkiewicz came to this meeting furious, may you think that there was yet another meeting when Loncar went to see Drewienkiewicz on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. And I think I would have known had this meeting been held. However, I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I don't know. Mr. Robinson, in the materials for Drewienkiewicz's evidence, in tab 72 of his testimony, he referred to the aide-memoire of the members of the army of Yugoslavia in the area that was covered by sabotage activity dated June 1998. I have the aide-memoire, but I did not particularly submit it to you because it was admitted during General Drewienkiewicz's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please place your copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a copy to be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Drewienkiewicz, during his testimony, interpreted some rules from this document. And can you tell me whether you were aware of this way of interpretation or, rather, were all members of the Kosovo Verification Mission that you were in contact with provided the same interpretation of these rules, and how does this interpretation differ from the interpretation of these same rules by members of the military? I'm referring to the interpretation of these rules and one's attitude towards what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This is a manual which was prepared by the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia engaged in the territory engulfed by sabotage and terrorist activities. It contains all international standards in this respect and rules that could be applied when anti-terrorist action is concerned. This manual and everything that is contained in it does not differ from internationally recognised standards in any way. So General Drewienkiewicz's analysis here, I believe, is not right. I think that he tried to interpret some things in his own way and to draw conclusions that would be contrary to international rules and to this manual of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this evidence is relevant at all it's confusing me because I'm not being reminded of what the interpretation was. I am not going to interrupt much or at all on the grounds of relevance. The accused will spend his limited time as he thinks fit, but I just don't see how this really can help us at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the relevance of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Drewienkiewicz testified here, as you were able to see, about certain examples, giving a totally different interpretation. And this is a manual for members of the army of Yugoslavia acting in areas engulfed in sabotage and terrorist activities. He said that certain provisions here were put very mildly, they were not binding enough. And I was going to ask our witness if this is a binding manual for members of the VJ or can it be interpreted in a flexible manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, what would you say about this evidence? It goes to the credibility of General DZ?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're just looking at it in the English on the exhibits that have been scanned, so we're looking at the document at the moment. It occurs to me that this is relevant to evidence given by DZ as to what the position was. This witness is entitled to comment upon that, which is the purpose of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The problem, though, is the accused hasn't put the question specifically enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if he can rephrase it, that may assist the Court. I don't know whether the Court's been able to get it in the English from the scanned exhibit to see it on their screen. We've been able to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, our network does not have the translated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ah, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will read to you what Drewienkiewicz said, and I will ask the witness to say whether it is so or not. Is this an official document from the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Drewienkiewicz says, on page 2980 of the transcript: "[In English] Well, if I can take you to the last page of the document which says what has to be done with this document. And it says that this memorandum shall be sent to the units at company -- at company and independent platoon level."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Even in a different courtroom with different machinery, Ms. Dicklich is invaluable in her ability to multi-task and she's managed to find this document on Sanction, which we have here on a separate screen. And if Sanction can be thrown up onto the system, you'll have it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be helpful, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have only the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the accused would let us know which page we should be looking at in the English, Ms. Dicklich will be able to oblige.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the page, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now quoting from what Drewienkiewicz said in his testimony. It would be good to show the first page of the original in the Serbian language to show what the cover page looks like. It's an official document of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. There is the Yugoslav coat of arms, it says: "Army of Yugoslavia. Reminder for Yugoslav army members engaged in areas affected by sabotage and terrorist activities." Now, Drewienkiewicz says that this reminder would be sent "[In English] at company and independent platoon level." [Interpretation] Is that the lowest tactical level that this reminder would reach?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that imply that everybody would be familiarised with it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, down to squad or platoon commander, which is the lowest level. The commander would be familiarised and thereby the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he says, going to the next paragraph, he quotes: "[In English] Systematically go through the entire reminder with all army members on the territory where sabotage and terrorist attack are conducted and proper individuals thus prepare individuals and units to implement the prescribed procedure." [Interpretation] All right. And then the quotation ends and he says and it finishes: "Officers in command positions shall be responsible for the consistent implementation of the reminder in their formations." He goes on: "[In English] This I think indicates that there was a set of rules to be followed in dealing with insurgents -- followed in dealing with insurgents," et cetera. [Interpretation] So what about this procedure? Did it encompass - and that is the important thing - all those who were active, who were engaged, as it says in the title, in areas affected by sabotage and terrorist activities, instructing them to act consistently with the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, that was ensured. And I said this reminder took into account all international standards regarding fight against terrorism. And speaking of this reminder, this insistence on page 4, which Drewienkiewicz commented upon, says: "Try to avoid use of weapons against members of terrorist groups." He said that this word "try to avoid" is too mild.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he quoted from the document himself, and I believe you can do that too. On page 2981 of the transcript, Drewienkiewicz quoted this document of the General Staff: "[In English] The following is forbidden: Killing detained persons; inflicting bodily harm on them; robbing detained persons, sick and wounded; desecrating corpses; looting them." [Interpretation] Then end of quotation. And he says on the next page, I think, quoting again: "[In English] Offending human dignity, rape and forced prostitution." [Interpretation] All this is written and he quoted it. And then comes what you just mentioned. Drewienkiewicz says on 2982: "If we go on to paragraph 4," again he quotes: "One should endeavour to avoid use of artillery weapons -- [In English] One should endeavour to avoid the use of artillery weapons and other weapons against citizens who are not offering any resistance, against places of worship, and the like. And that, again, is what one would hope to see, but the word 'endeavour' -- the word 'endeavour' again I would draw your attention to, because I think it should be written that every effort ought to be taken to." [Interpretation] And then again under quotation marks: "'Endeavour' is, frankly, weak in this sort of context, in my view."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for a question and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Drewienkiewicz criticised this reminder, which contains - and he quoted a lot from it - a lot of orders and bans, and this wording, translated into English as "endeavour" or "making an effort" as related to the use of artillery weapons. Would you interpret it as allowing you to use artillery weapons because the word "endeavour" is so mild?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This concept does not differ in any way from the wording Drewienkiewicz recommended as fitting. In our interpretation of the word "endeavour," it is exactly the same as what he recommended. It does not say at any point that something like this could be done without taking any measures to avoid casualties. I don't see the difference, the distinction that he was trying to make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, is there any difference between this protocol of edition to Geneva Conventions, 12th of August, 1949, relating to the protection of victims of international armed conflict, protocol I, and Article 57 that says: "In the conduct of military operations [In English] care shall be taken to spare the civilian population, civilians and civilian objects." [Interpretation] Does this wording of the Geneva Convention or, rather, the protocol to the Geneva Convention, differ in any way from what is written in this reminder if we say, "In the conduct of military operations, constant care shall be taken to spare the civilian population, civilians, and civilian objects?" Is that the same thought expressed in this reminder, or is Mr. Drewienkiewicz right in saying that this is not emphatic enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see any difference between what Drewienkiewicz is saying and our word "endeavour." I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how much longer will you be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I planned to finish today, including the cross-examination, but unfortunately this is proceeding a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to assist the Court. The last section we were on was on page 8 of the English document, where the word "endeavour" was. My Sanction connection went. I don't know if everyone else still had it, but it was page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must consider whether you need to ask all these questions of this witness in relation to General DZ's testimony. You do have a right to have your witness comment on the testimony if you're seeking to contradict the witness, the witness's testimony, but I don't know how much importance is to be attached to General DZ's testimony. So you need to consider whether you need to spend so much time with this witness on that aspect. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Record-keeping and exhibits, as promised. The Court probably has two documents, one in ordinary portrait format, headed Exhibits to be used with Milan Kotur, some clearly not exhibited and others marked as documents, for example, D300, tabs 165 and so on, not admitted. It seems to us that that is an accurate reflection of the state of those documents which were to be found in the binders provided by the accused. Similarly accurate appears to us to be the other document, I think provided by the pro se liaison officer, dealing with documents that the accused wanted to be considered or looked at, having been produced by or through Delic. They are either all been produced, or it may be - and we haven't been able to check this - some of them are produced for identification subject to production of final translations. So these two documents would appear to be accurate and satisfactory to work from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice, yes. Mr. Milosevic, do you want all the documents to be admitted from -- until number 15?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I omitted some tabs. I did omit some tabs. But just the ones I mentioned, because there are a number of diagrams and schematics contained in the documents. I don't think they need all be admitted. I just mentioned the ones that I would like to have admitted and the ones commented on by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 167 will be admitted. Those are the ones --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 16 onwards, all of them admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And from tab 16 to 68 will be admitted. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let's try to have your examination-in-chief concluded as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm doing my best, Mr. Robinson, and I am bearing in mind your suggestion, and I don't need to deal with Drewienkiewicz at such great length, but I would just like to mention one more question and that was something that he raised as well as some other witnesses of the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3016, he says the following, and I'm going to quote a short passage from the transcript: "[In English] Therefore, FRY forces -- when FRY forces responded, it was our opinion that that response should be proportionate, and it quite often wasn't and therefore we would report it as being disproportionate." [Interpretation] Now, Colonel, he here implicitly confirms the fact that our forces did react and respond to KLA attacks, but the problem was -- and he doesn't challenge that, but the problem was that it was disproportionate. Now, did you consider this question with the representatives of the Verification Mission? Did you bring that up, this disproportionate alleged response on the part of our side, and did our side act disproportionately and often, as he says so here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: As regards our response to the provocations or attacks of the so-called Liberation Army of Kosovo and Metohija, we did our best to ensure that it be a proportionate response as far as was possible, that is to say to protect us from the attacks. And you're going to find that stipulated in the daily report sent to the liaison team and the General Staff. There were at meetings -- at two or three meetings times when this question was raised of proportionate and disproportionate response, looking at the number of persons killed, number of persons taken prisoner, and that he doubted that this was proportionate, although he did say that our response was justified, and so on and so forth. But that's where it ended. It stopped there. What I can tell you is this: We did take care that our response should be proportionate and adequate and commensurate with the attack to protect our units or facilities or features or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you attended the first meeting with Walker, who otherwise led -- was led by General Loncar on our side in Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what can you tell us about that meeting? What was the subject of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, at the first official meeting that General Loncar chaired and led on behalf of the federal committee for relations with the Verification Mission, the composition of which was the representatives of the MUP, Colonel Mijatovic and I myself, and an interpreter from the foreign affairs department, and that was held at the headquarters of the Verification Mission in Pristina. And at the meeting Mr. Walker told Mr. Loncar or, rather, he apologised right at the beginning of the meeting because he had taken up the retirement time which would otherwise have let him play with his grandchildren, and that he was to blame because, he said, that at a meeting with Milosevic in Belgrade he happened to remember Mr. Loncar and their cooperation dating back to the Slavonia days and he wished to work with somebody who he knew. And so it was at his request that Mr. Milosevic enabled him to do so and to meet Loncar. So that was the beginning of the meeting. At the meeting itself, we presented our structure and the make-up of our team and the liaison man for Kosovo and Metohija. We decided upon our guidelines for cooperation about verification of events and matters of that kind during that first initial contact, as much as we were able to present. He was alone, just with an interpreter. He didn't have his advisors there with him. And then Mr. Walker informed us of a meeting that he had had before arriving in Pristina with you, and he told us that he was surprised how far Mr. Milosevic lacked knowledge and information about the situation prevailing in Kosovo and Metohija. He also said that he was even more surprised of the way in which Mr. Milosevic interpreted the agreement signed by our government with the OSCE with respect to the establishment of a Verification Mission in Kosovo and Metohija and its work. So that, in the briefest terms, were the contents of that meeting of ours. We decided at the meeting or, rather, General Loncar asked me to speak on behalf of the Pristina Corps and Colonel Mijatovic on behalf of MUP. That's what was proposed, and the general mood was friendly between Loncar and Drewienkiewicz. It was established that the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mean Drewienkiewicz or Walker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, I meant Walker, sorry. So that Mr. Loncar and Mr. Walker held the discussions themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You've now described to us that first meeting. As a witness here, Mr. Walker said that it is not -- "My assertion is not true that General Loncar was appointed to his position in Kosovo and Metohija at his request." May we have your comments on that assertion made by William Walker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, that assertion doesn't hold water because, as I said at the beginning, he apologised to begin with, said it was his wish to cooperate with Loncar and his fault for separating Loncar from his days as a pensioner, carefree days of enjoying his retirement. That's what he said to him personally and apologised to him for pulling him out of retirement, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Otherwise, he said: "I did not ask for General Loncar. As I say, I only inquired about someone we both knew [In English] as a means of getting the conversation started. But as I also said, I was really quite surprised when I got to Kosovo a few days later and found General Loncar there representing the government, especially since I'd been told he was in retirement and his whereabouts were unknown to the president." [Interpretation] Does that explanation of his stand?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. It's not the correct one, not truthful. What I said is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to another area with respect to Walker. He said that he received the first information about Racak from General Loncar and that General Loncar was not present during the visit to Racak and that he called General Loncar -- he invited General Loncar to go with him but that the man didn't accept. Now, do you know anything about that, why Loncar didn't want to go, didn't go to Racak with Walker or didn't want to Racak with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: First of all, nobody invited or asked Loncar to go to Racak. I know that for sure. And that can also be seen from the minutes and records that we read of the 16th of January meeting where Mr. Drewienkiewicz had a meeting with Loncar and myself. And Walker was already in Racak at that time. Secondly, the first piece of information that something was going on in Racak or not I was asked to give by Mr. Drewienkiewicz on the 15th in the evening, somewhere around 2330 hours -- or 2330 hours, I'm sorry. Yes. And I think I said that in my previous response. Loncar couldn't have informed Walker, because Walker was elsewhere, travelling in Montenegro or in Skopje or somewhere. And so the first information that could have reached him, it was logical to suppose, could have just come from Mr. Drewienkiewicz as his deputy. And in the afternoon in Pec where he held a meeting with his verifiers, Mr. Drewienkiewicz heard about this action, although it was announced earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So Walker spoke about an attack here of a drunken policeman, an attack at members of the mission and said that he considered that his safety and security and that of his team was jeopardised, and he asked Loncar to conduct an investigation, which Loncar agreed to do, promised to do. Later on allegedly Loncar said to him that Walker and the others had dreamt up this whole thing, fabricated it, because they had provoked the policeman and the whole incident happened in quite a different way from what Walker described it. So that's what he says in his testimony on page 6838 -- or 37 and 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Well, I do know something about that because the building where the mission had its headquarters and the building in which Mr. Walker was accommodated borders on -- is next door to the MUP meeting in Pristina, and it is true that a policeman did try to get up close to Walker, but nothing more than that. That's all that happened. But soon afterwards, Walker seemed to have raised this incident to a higher level, adding to it more than was truthful, with the desire to allow his security men to arm themselves, because they didn't have an armed escort. So there were polemics over this armed escort subject. But that's where the whole incident finished. It wasn't an important incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody in fact attack him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No, nobody attacked him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Walker, on page 6867, says that he did not receive information about Racak on the afternoon of the 15th because he was in Montenegro throughout the day, but he heard about Racak for the first time when he later returned to Pristina, when Drewienkiewicz came to see him and told him that somebody had communicated with him from Loncar's office and informed him that a conflict had taken place with the KLA in Racak. Can you confirm that? Do you know anything about Racak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: So this confirms it. It confirms who Drewienkiewicz communicated with, which is me, from Loncar's office, because my office and Loncar's office are next door to each other, and incoming calls would be passed on to me if Loncar wasn't there. Now that Drewienkiewicz said to him first, said this to Walker first, that would be logical because he was his deputy, Walker's deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you inform Drewienkiewicz that an incident in Racak had taken place or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Drewienkiewicz asked me something about the event in Racak on the 15th in the evening at 2330 hours. But he already knew about the event; he just wanted to talk to me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us about that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6690 or, rather, 6900, he said that they kept asking police commanders about information as to how many policemen, how many soldiers, tanks, weapons, artillery pieces they had, so that they could assess whether the number was growing, getting smaller, or stayed the same. Do you have any comments to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't really know. They knew how many weapons we had, how much weaponry we had. There was no need for them to ask us, because according to a report, we read that in Kosovska Mitrovica they had a whole infrastructure with all the established units, a full complement of units and they knew all about that, so it wasn't something that was unknown, not an unknown quantity, because all the information about the situation in our army, the units of our army, were stored in the controls department in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that the agreement was not acted upon according to which the army was duty-bound to inform of troop movements, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again the interpreter is asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said despite that obligation, members of the KVM often came across tanks in streets, moving in various directions of which the verifiers were not informed. So what is the truth in all of this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: The truth is this: They were informed about all and every movement on the part of our units, and you can see this from the daily reports that were written. So there was not a single troop movement that they weren't informed of. And we had no reason not to inform them about it. So that these tanks roaming around the streets and all the rest of it is a little ludicrous, if I might say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, the witness of the opposite side, Mr. Ciaglinski -- you know who he is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He brought up a few things here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Ciaglinski partly testified in closed session, and I would like to ask you for this to be discussed in open session, but I cannot present the arguments for that in open session because I don't know what your ultimate ruling will be. So could I please ask you to move into private session for a moment so that you would see what this is about, and I hope that you will agree that this can be discussed indeed in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We'll hear your arguments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I suggest that we ask the witness after all, does he agree to have this in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now we are in open session again. Thank you for having allowed to deal with this in open session. On transcript page 3218, Ciaglinski speaks of some meeting with you and others. I'm not going to go into all of this right now, but I have to read part of the transcript. "Question: At the conclusion of that meeting, did something occur that was particularly noteworthy to you? "Yes. I was given some information which I found rather surprising." Question again: "And without disclosing the name of the individual who provided that information, can you tell us the general circumstances about how it was that you had an opportunity to get this additional information? "At the conclusion of one of our meetings, when most of the members who had taken part in this meeting had departed, myself and my interpreter met with this official, and he put a map on the table and began telling us exactly what the future options were for Kosovo. "Mr. Ryneveld: Might we move briefly into private session. "Judge May: Yes." [Interpretation] And then it says "Private session." [In English]. "Question: Once we've been assured that your comments can now not be heard by anyone -- are we at that stage? "Registrar: Yes. "We are in private session. "Sir, who was the individual who you met with in the presence of your interpreter, who spread out the map? "Answer: Colonel Kotur. "Question: And just so that we know who he was, he was the gentleman who had been part of the commission for some time? "Answer: Yes. He was -- he was there right from the very beginning, as the -- sort of the main VJ, serving VJ officer on the commission who had in fact disappeared ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must ask a question now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought that I should read out the transcript and then to get a response to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you've already read enough. Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, is this correct, what Ciaglinski said here, that when the meeting was over, when you were alone with him, that you spread out this map and gave him some kind of explanations? After all, in all fairness, there are other explanations that he gives in terms of what he -- you said to him. But tell me, did you spread out a map and give him some information as to what the intentions of the army of Yugoslavia were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. I did not spread a map out for him. I did not give him any kind of explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Further on he says: "[In English] ... right from the very beginning as the -- sort of the main VJ, serving VJ officer on the commission who had in fact disappeared when the -- who had --" [Interpretation] who actually -- "[In English] -- Brankovic Commission came in but occasionally put in an appearance again. "And he was present at this particular -- "He was present at this meeting, and what happened was that it was just himself, my interpreter and myself present when these discussions took place." Again another question: "What level was he with the VJ? "Well, he was an extremely experienced officer who had served for more than ten years, possibly as much as 15 years in Kosovo, had a house in Kosovo and had been -- had taken part in the activities in 1998 as a commander in the Djakovica area where various events, fairly serious fighting, took place." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. "[In English]... the type of uniform he wore ... he tended to wear a special forces uniform but he was very well informed, very well --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please put a question. You're not using your time well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What he says here, that for ten or 15 years you were in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That's correct. I was in Kosovo for ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he puts a question to you: Who were you directly subordinated to, and you said General Loncar. So according to what he said here, you explained to him -- rather, the rest is in public session. There is no mention of your name, but it says what you had said, and it says here, it's written down in the transcript: "This official spread the map on the table in front of me, and without any preamble at all, he told me exactly how the plan to deal with the KLA would take place." [Interpretation] And then Ryneveld gives him some kind of map, some ordinary map of Kosovo. Never mind. And he gives him some green markers so that he could show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are wasting time. What is your question? If you don't have any other questions for the witness, then we'll move to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to read this out, what Colonel Kotur allegedly said to him. That's what it says here on page 3222. Right. Basically it's a quote allegedly from Mr. Kotur. "Basically we are going to carry on our operations from Vucitrn and push the KLA across towards Glogovac. At Glogovac there is a large force of --" this was where -- [Interpretation] and so on. T72 and T84. "[In English] We will then cut off and destroy any stragglers that manage to make it over the hill towards Glogovac." [Interpretation] He talks about Podujevo and Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what turns on this issue, Mr. Milosevic, as to whether Colonel Kotur said this to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what turns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to Ciaglinski? What is the issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is at issue is that Ciaglinski is obviously lying, and then he says that Kotur said to him -- "[In English] And when we have finished dealing with the KLA, we will remove all the Albanians from the territory of Kosovo forever."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's it. Okay. So put that to the witness as to whether he -- put that to the witness, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's exactly what I've been doing, reading this. This is astonishing. That's why I'm reading it. I want him to hear what had been said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Colonel, you heard the description that Ciaglinski gave of that meeting of yours. Did you actually stay with Ciaglinski one-on-one? Did you spread out a map? Did you say that, "We're going to expel the KLA, and that after that we're going to expel the Albanians forever"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That is a pure lie. I said none of this to Ciaglinski. Why he invented all of this is something I really don't understand. Secondly, he also invented that I had disappeared from the team for relations with the Verification Mission. That's a lie too. There was a change. There was a reorganisation of the team for relations with the Verification Mission, but that was only on the 10th of March, ten days prior to the departure of the Kosovo Verification Mission from Kosovo. I had my last meeting with Mr. Ciaglinski on the 10th of March. I have a copy of the minutes of that meeting here, and it was included in this binder where these tabs are. I don't know exactly which tab it is, but I can't find it. And at that meeting on the 10th of March, I tell him that many officers, professional officers, came, 26 of them, and that from the -- from the 10th of March onwards we have new people, new professionals in Kosovo and Metohija. Until then, liaison officers, in addition to conducting their regular duties, worked as liaison officers as well. So on the 12th of March I was given an assignment by General Loncar, to make sure that the delegation of Albanians be sent to Rambouillet by French aircraft. And on the 13th I was personally present at the airport, guaranteeing that this transportation would be conducted properly. So I was active until the very last day, as far as the mission was concern -- or, rather, the team for relations with missions in Kosovo. So it's not that I disappeared. What Ciaglinski is saying is not the case. I would like that to be clear on the basis of the record from the 10th of March. I believe that you have it in your materials there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you to look it up by tomorrow, regardless of whether we finish now or not. You don't have to dwell on that right this instant. And now for something completely different. Ciaglinski said here that he was denied accession to FRY forces, that basically he had been turned down. He said that if patrols of verifiers or, rather, teams from the ground would return to him, he would contact the mission for cooperation and seek access for the mission on the ground. He would address Loncar or you, Colonel Kotur. Is it correct that he was not allowed access to the forces of the FRY and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: That's not correct. There was not a single question that Ciaglinski raised in front of me and that I could not and did not resolve to our mutual satisfaction. So touring units in the area and some units in the border belt, control of the border units, touring border posts, in-depth security units, we did all of that together. And I repeat once again, not a single subject that he raised before the team of the Pristina Corps was not seen through. I'm not saying that at lower levels and at regional centres officers for liaison and battalions, et cetera -- well, things happen, but Mr. Ciaglinski, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, I, Mr. Loncar, all of this was carried out in the field. So that's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. He talked about winter training or, rather, winter exercises [In English] in relation to your duty in Kosovo, a term that is known to you. [Interpretation] He says that he drew the attention of persons responsible in the army that this was a violation of the agreement and the response he got that they had to train because their training ground is actually the area of Kosovo. Was this a violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR
utterances.text: This was not a violation of the agreement. They actually agreed, Ciaglinski did. I'll show you the record tomorrow. They agreed that this was a normal reaction on our part, that it was only natural that we should train our troops, and that the only problem was that they saw that through this training of our units we were irritating the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army and, being irritated, they could attack us, we could respond, and then there could be a conflagration. I think that on the 15th of February - I'm not sure about this, I looked at one of my work notebooks during these past few days and I think it found it there - Mr. Ciaglinski went to Brussels to report at the NATO command there about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. He said that the presentation was positive, that it was in our favour, and I think that Mr. Vollebaek, as a matter of fact, when he came to Kosovo and Metohija, he conveyed our view of the situation, that we view the KLA as a terrorist organisation, and then we had these NATO threats, and anyway, he said that what we were doing was legitimate and all right. Vollebaek, he said, was even surprised by this position and that he was actually surprised by how he was presenting our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
